title: THE ASSESSING OFFICER, TEXTILES COMMITTEE VS. M/S. PREMIUM SUITING PVT. LTD.

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1158
Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 1 of 17
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 785 OF 2016
THE ASSESSING OFFICER,
TEXTILES COMMITTEE ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
M/S. PREMIUM SUITING PVT. LTD.
& ANOTHER ...RESPONDENTS

J U D G M E N T
N.V. ANJARIA, J.
 The present appeal preferred by the Assessing Officer,
Textile Committee, is directed against order dated
06.03.2013 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad1 in Writ Tax No. 354 of 2006, whereby the High
Court allowed the writ petition of the respondent No.1
herein.
2. The writ petition was filed challenging order dated
20.10.2005 passed by the Textiles Committee Cess
Appellate Tribunal2 in T.C.A. No. 223 of 2002. The Appellate
1 Hereinafter "High Court"
2 Hereinafter "Appellate Tribunal"

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 2 of 17
Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the respondent No.1 herein
and upheld the order of the assessing authority demanding
textile cess to the tune of Rs. 2,68,293/-. The High Court
quashed the textile cess demand.
3. The facts may be outlined. The appellant-Textiles
Committee is a statutory body under Section 3 of the
Textiles Committee Act, 19633 functioning under the
Ministry of Textiles, Government of India with an object to
ensure the quality of textiles and textile machinery, whereas
respondent No.1 is a company engaged in the
manufacturing of textiles. The respondent No.1 is engaged
in bleaching, dyeing and processing of 100% man-made
fabrics, supplied by powerloom and handloom units.
3.1 It appears that a letter dated 28.06.2001 came to be
written from the office of Comptroller General of India to the
Ministry of Textiles stating inter alia that in the course of the
audit, it was found that out of 30 independent textiles
processors, only one processor had been paying the cess
during 2000-2001 in 5 Commissionerates of Central Excise
3 Hereinafter 'Act'

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 3 of 17
of Uttar Pradesh and that the remaining 29 processors did
not pay the cess which according to the office of Comptroller
General of India was of the value of Rs.39.64 lacs during
1997 to 2000.
3.2 In pursuance of the aforementioned communication,
respondent No.1 herein was served with show cause notice
dated 20.08.2001 by the appellant-assessing officer, raising
demand of Rs.2,68,293/- towards textile cess. The show
cause notice was replied to on 28.08.2001. Respondent
No.1's claim for exemption from payment of cess was not
accepted by the authorities. Respondent No.1 had
submitted in the reply that its unit was an independent
textile processor for the textiles manufactured received from
the powerloom industries and it was on job work basis. It
was stated that the textile (fabric) was made by small
weavers in the small household industries which had
powerlooms below 50 in numbers in all cases and that they
did not have any spinning plants. It was contended that the
Act provided and exempted all the products from the
purview of applicability of the cess and the cess was not
payable.

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 4 of 17
3.3 As the explanation of the appellant was not accepted,
the assessment order dated 21.11.2001 came to be passed
by the competent authority fixing the liability on respondent
No.1 to pay textile cess to the tune of Rs.2,68,293/-. The
inspecting officer by his letter dated 16.10.2001 clarified
that the powerloom/handloom fabrics were exempted from
cess only at the loom stage and not afterwards when they
are further processed. Respondent No.1-company, aggrieved
by the demand notice and the assessment orders,
approached the Appellate Tribunal by filing Appeal No. 223
of 2002.
3.4 The Appellate Tribunal relied on its own decision in
Chandok Textile Exporters Pvt. Ltd. vs. Assessing
Officer, Textites Committee in T.C.A. No. 222 of 2002
on 30.04.2004 holding that the processing activity
amounted to manufacturing under the Act and the job
workers and the merchant dealers were jointly and severally
liable to pay cess under the Act. The view taken in that case
was that the processing fabrics out of powerloom and
handloom industries for further manufacturing was not
exempted under the Proviso to Section 5A of the Act. With

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 5 of 17
such reasoning, entirely based on its own decision in
Chandok Textile Exporters Pvt. Ltd. (supra), the Appellate
Tribunal dismissed the appeal of respondent No.1 on
09.12.2005.
3.5 Respondent No.1 was required to deposit the
adjudicated amount of Rs.2,68,293/-. Another notice dated
06.01.2006 was also issued to respondent No.1 which was
a separate cause of action, wherein demand for payment of
Rs.1,43,176/- towards textile cess was raised in respect of
the period from April 2001 to December 2003. Against the
order of dismissal of the appeal by the Appellate Tribunal,
the respondent-company preferred writ before the High
Court. While allowing the writ petition of respondent No.1
herein, the High Court held that the activity of bleaching and
dyeing and other processing of power unit or handloom
textiles by job workers would not mean obliteration of the
status of textile as products of the powerloom industry and
since such powerloom textiles are exempted from payment
of textiles tax under Section 5A of the Act, the tax would not
be payable.

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 6 of 17
3.5.1 It was further reasoned that the job workers
perform an extended activity for the manufacturers,
observing,
 'The hand-loom and power-loom textile
manufacturers instead of getting work of bleaching
etc. done by themselves, have engaged the petitioner
on job work basis. The petitioner received the textile
and after doing the needful return the textile to such
manufacturers. Section 5A imposes cess for the
purposes of the Act, 1963, a duty of excise on all
textiles and on all textile machinery manufactured in
India. The word 'manufacture' is not defined in the
Act, 1963.'
3.5.2 The High Court further stated,
 'Since the textile manufactured out from hand-loom and power-loom industry has been exempted
under section 5A, obviously no inspection in respect
of textile manufactured by such industry is required
and therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the
activity undertaken by an extended hand of these
manufacturers will also be not liable to pay the impost
of cess under the Act.'
4. Heard learned counsel Mr. Chirag M. Shroff for the
appellant and learned counsel Mr. Tanmaya Agarwal for
respondent No.1.
5. The Textile authority seeks to derive its power to levy
cess under Section 5A of the Act, inserted by Act 51 of 1973,

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 7 of 17
with effect from 01.01.1975, Section 5A is extracted
hereunder,
5A. Imposition of cess on textiles and textile
machinery manufactured in India.-(1) There shall
be levied and collected as a cess for the purposes of this
Act a duty of excise on all textiles and on all textile
machinery manufactured in India at such rate, not
exceeding one per cent. ad valorem as the Central
Government may, by notification in the Official
Gazette, fix:
Provided that no such cess shall be levied on textiles
manufactured from out of handloom or powerloom
industry.
(2) The duty of excise levied under sub-section (1) shall
be in addition to any cess or duty leviable on textiles or
textile machinery under any other law for the time
being in force.
(3) The duty of excise levied under sub-section (1) shall
be collected by the Committee, in accordance with the
rules made in this behalf, from every manufacturer of
textiles or textile machinery (hereinafter in this section
and in sections 5C and 5D referred to as the
manufacturer).
(4) The manufacturer shall pay to the Committee the
amount of the duty of excise levied under sub-section
(1) within one month from the date on which he
receives a notice of demand therefore from the
Committee.
(5) For the purpose of enabling the Committee to assess
the amount of the duty of excise levied under sub-section (1),-
(a) the Committee shall, by notification in the
Gazette of India, fix the period in respect of which
assessments shall be made; and
(b) every manufacturer shall furnish to the
Committee a return, not later than fifteen days
after the expiry of the period to which the return

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 8 of 17
relates, specifying the total quantity of textiles or
textile machinery manufactured by him during
the said period and such other particulars as may
be prescribed.
(6) If asssny manufacturer fails to furnish the return
referred to in sub-section (5) within the time specified
therein, or furnishes a return which the Committee has
reason to believe is incorrect or defective, the
Committee may assess the amount of the duty of excise
in such manner as may be prescribed.
(7) Any manufacturer aggrieved by an assessment
made under this section may appeal to the Tribunal,
constituted under section 5B for cancellation or
modification of the assessment.
5.1 Section 5A contemplates levy and collection of cess on
all textiles and all textile machinery manufactured in India.
A manufacturer of textiles becomes liable to pay the cess by
virtue of Section 5A. The provision is applied in case of
respondent No.1 herein. The text of Section 5A has at its
several places the phrase 'textile manufactured', however,
the word 'manufacture' is not defined in the Act.
5.2 The word 'textile' is defined in the Act in Section 2(g).
The said definition is as under,
2. Definitions.-In this Act, unless there is anything
repugnant in the subject or context,-
(g) 'textiles' means any fabric or cloth or yarn or
garment or any other article made wholly or
in part of-

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 9 of 17
(i) cotton; or
(ii) wool; or
(iii) silk; or
(iv) artificial silk or other fiber,
and includes fiber;
5.3 The word 'powerloom' is defined in Section 2(da) to
mean a loom which is worked by power as defined in clause
(g) of Section 2 of the Factories Act and which is used or
capable of being used for weaving cloth wholly or partly out
of the cotton yarn or wollen yarn, or fibre, or any kind of
mixed yarn. The definition of powerloom industry is defined
in Section 2(db) to mean an industry in which a
manufacturer of textiles has during the period not more
than 50 powerlooms in the factory.
5.4 Now, the High Court in the impugned order dealt with
the argument advanced on behalf of appellant-Textiles
Committee that although the word 'manufacture' has not
been defined in Act, the definition of the word 'manufacture'
found in Section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 19444 should
be adopted and applied which inter alia contemplates that
the concept of 'manufacture' includes any process incidental
4 Hereinafter 'Central Excise Act'

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 10 of 17
or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product.
On the basis of such argument, it was sought to be
suggested that the bleaching and dyeing was the process
incidental to the completion of manufactured product,
therefore, the same would have to be construed as
'manufacture' to apply Section 5A of the Act, consequently,
the levy of textile cess was legal and justified.
5.5 This Court endorses to the view taken by the High
Court in the above count namely that unless the particular
word of section is included to be read by virtue of reference
or incorporation from the other statute, such word cannot
be readily taken as applicable in the statute where it is not
defined. The High Court was correct in relying on the
decision of this Court in Union of India and Others vs. R.C.
Jain and Others5
, in which it is held that if a particular
expression is not defined in an Act, its definition in another
Act cannot be imported into the former Act.
5.6 It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that
a particular word or a phrase or a section in any enactment
5
(1981) 2 SCS 308

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 11 of 17
has to be construed, interpreted and applied having regard
to the context of the scheme, purpose and operational ambit
of such statute. Every statute has in its subject matter as a
distinguished context. Therefore, the same word occurring
in the other statute cannot be bodily lifted and read as
defined in the other statute for the purpose of applying the
same, unless such word or definition or provision is provided
to be read by the legislature by applying doctrine of reference
or doctrine of incorporation.
5.7 The following observations by this Court in Jagatram
Ahuja vs. Commissioner of Gift Tax, Hyderabad6
, are on
the same lines,
'...the words and expressions defined in one statute as
judicially interpreted do not afford a guide to
construction of the same words or expressions in
another statute unless both the statutes are pari
materia legislations or it is specifically so provided in
one statute to give the same meaning to the words as
defined in the other statute. The aim and object of the
two legislations, namely, the Gift Tax Act and the
Estate Duty Act are not similar.'
(Para 23)
6
(2000) 8 SCC 249

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 12 of 17
5.8 In Maheshwari Fish Seed Farm vs. T.N. Electricity
Board and Another7
, the argument before this Court on
behalf of the appellant was that the word 'agriculture' as
defined in the blank Act, should follow the same meaning as
defined in other Act such as Tamil Nadu Agricultural
Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1987, Tamil Nadu
Agriculture University Act, 1971 or Agriculture and Rural
Debt Relief Scheme, 1990 in which the term 'agriculture'
included 'pisciculture'.
5.8.1 The Court said that it was not permissible to
assign similar meaning of the definition of a particular word
in one statute, to the definition of the very word in the other
statute,
'...Suffice it to observe that the common-parlance
meaning of the term 'agriculture', in the context in
which it has been used and is arising for
determination before us, cannot be determined by
reference to definitions given in other statutes. This
we say for more reasons than one. Firstly, none of the
statutes referred to by Shri Iyer, the learned Senior
Counsel, can be called statutes in pari materia.
Secondly, it is common knowledge that the definition
coined by the legislature for the purpose of a
particular enactment is often an extended or artificial
meaning so assigned as to fulfil the object of that
enactment. Such definitions given in other
enactments cannot be freely used for finding out
7
(2004) 4 SCC 705

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 13 of 17
meaning to be assigned to a term of common parlance
used in an altogether different setting.'
(Para 16)
5.8.2 The Court quoted with approval from 'Principles
of Statutory Interpretation' by Justice G.P. Singh [9th
Edition, 2004, Page 163] that 'it is hazardous to interpret a
statute in accordance with a definition in another statute
and more so when such statute is not dealing with any
cognate subject or the statutes are not in pari materia.'
6. The whole stand on the part of the textile authorities
in subjecting that the activity of the respondent-company
was liable to be treated as 'manufacture', is that when the
fabrics come from the powerloom or handloom industry to
the unit of respondent No.1, a process is undertaken in the
nature of bleaching, dyeing, etc. It is the case that when the
process is undergone on the fabric, in view of the definition
of manufacture in the other Acts, especially under the
Excise Act such as the Central Excise Act, process of
bleaching etc. would fall within the purview of
'manufacture'.

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 14 of 17
6.1 As already stated above, the word 'manufacture' is not
defined in the Act, and it is neither safe nor permissible in
law to advert to and adopt the connotation 'manufacture'
as defined in another statute, and on the basis of such alien
definition, treat the activity undertaken by respondent No.1
to be the manufacturing activity. Therefore, while
interpreting the word 'manufactured' which occurs in
Section 5A of the Act in the present case, it has to be
understood in its common parlance and not in any special
sense by borrowing a special ingredient of the concept from
other statute.
6.2 The Act provides for imposition of cess on textiles and
textile machinery 'manufactured'. The question is whether
the dyeing, bleaching, and such processing on the fabric
becomes 'textile manufactured' to attract the liability of cess.
The entire process that takes place in the instant case is that
the processor units of the respondent-company are
independent units for the processing of textile. The textile is
received from the handloom and powerloom textile
manufacturers which manufacture the textile.

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 15 of 17
6.3 These manufacturers of textiles do undertake work of
bleaching, dyeing etc. by themselves. They engage the
respondent-company for applying such kind of work on the
fabrics. Respondent No.1 is engaged by the powerloom and
handloom industries on job work basis. Job work is done by
respondent No.1 on behalf of the textile manufacturers. The
respondent-company gets the textile and, after applying
dyeing, bleaching and doing such processing as may be
needed, returns the textile to the powerloom manufacturers.
No 'manufacturing' takes place at the end of or by
respondent No.1. The product that comes out from the
assistant but independent unit of respondent No.1, is not
and the same could be termed or treated as 'textile
manufactured'.
6.4 Section 5A of the Act imposes textile cess, however, the
Proviso says that no such cess shall be levied on textiles
manufactured out of handloom or powerloom industry. In
another words, the textiles manufactured by the handloom
or powerloom industrial units cannot be subjected to levy of
textile cess. An express exemption is granted under Section
5A of the Act.

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 16 of 17
6.5 Respondent No.1 in its processing units does not
manufacture. It only processes the fabric or textile received
from the powerloom or handloom industry and, after dyeing
and bleaching, returns the same to the powerloom industry.
The activity undertaken by respondent No.1 is an extended
activity which refines the textile by applying dyeing and
bleaching. It could be viewed as an activity supplementary
and ancillary to the manufacturing of textiles which is
performed by the powerloom industry, which again is
exempted from textile tax under Section 5A of the Act.
6.6 Respondent No.1 through operation of its independent
processing units, operates only to the benefit of the textile
manufacturers in the powerloom industry. Its activity does
not fall within the concept of manufacture. Respondent No.1
only works as an extended arm for the manufacturers of the
textile of the powerloom industry. The fabric or textile which
becomes material bleached and dyed is not 'textile
manufactured'.
6.7 At the best, it is the textile upgraded, not to become
'manufacture' in its sense as could be applied in the context

Civil Appeal No. 785 of 2016 Page 17 of 17
of Section 5A in particular and for the purpose of context of
the Act in general. It has to be held that respondent No.1
cannot be subjected to and cannot be made liable to pay the
textile cess, as there is no 'textile manufactured' in its units.
7. For the reasons stated above, the challenge to the
impugned order of the High Court has to necessarily fail.
The appeal is meritless. The same is dismissed.
 Any interlocutory application, if pending, shall cease to
survive in view of the disposal of the appeal.
...............................J.
 [S.V.N. BHATTI]
...............................J.
 [N.V. ANJARIA]
NEW DELHI;
OCTOBER 26, 2026.
